title: 2026 Jeep Recon özellikleri, fiyatı ve performans detayları açıklandı
summary: Tamamen elektrikli 2026 Jeep Recon, 670 beygir güç sunan motoru ve 68.990 dolardan başlayan fiyatıyla tanıtıldı.
body:
Car and Driver tarafından detaylı test sürüşüne tabi tutulan tamamen elektrikli **2026 Jeep Recon**, markanın off-road mirasını elektrikli gelecekle buluşturuyor. Kutu biçimli profili, kare farları ve aydınlatmalı yedi slotlu klasik Jeep ızgarasıyla dikkat çeken araç, 68.990 dolardan başlayan fiyat etiketiyle kullanıcı karşısına çıkıyor. Dört tekerlekten çekiş sağlayan iki adet elektrik motoru sayesinde toplam 670 beygir güç ve 620 libre-fit tork üreten model, fabrika verilerine göre 0'dan 60 mil hıza 3,6 saniyede ulaşıyor.

## Tasarım ve iç mekan özellikleri

Wrangler modellerine kıyasla daha lüks bir iç mekana sahip olan 2026 Jeep Recon, kareye yakın bir direksiyon simidi ve 14,5 inç boyutunda büyük bir dokunmatik ekran barındırıyor. Araçta alet gerektirmeden çıkarılabilen dört kapı ve arka camlar yer alıyor; ancak yaklaşık 32 kilo ağırlığındaki kapıların araç içinde saklanması için özel bir alan bulunmuyor. İkinci sıranın arkasında 30 fit küp kargo alanı sunan model, ön bagajında (frunk) ise ek 3 fit küp depolama kapasitesi sağlıyor. 94 kWh kapasiteli bataryayla donatılan aracın Moab donanım paketinde tahmini menzili 222 mil olarak belirtiliyor.

## Yol tutuşu ve şarj performansı

Asfaltta Wrangler modellerine göre çok daha kararlı bir direksiyon ve yol tutuşu sergileyen Recon, test pistinde 60 mil hıza 3,5 saniyede ulaştı. Arazide çelik batarya koruma plakaları, elektronik kilitlenebilir arka diferansiyel ve 24 inç suya batma derinliği gibi özelliklerle iddialı olan araç, yüzde 10'dan yüzde 80 şarj seviyesine ortalama 107 kW güçla 43 dakikada ulaşıyor. 

**Neden önemli?** Geleneksel off-road yeteneklerini tamamen elektrikli bir altyapıyla birleştiren 2026 Jeep Recon, sunduğu yüksek performans ve sökülebilir parçalara sahip açık kabin tasarımıyla elektrikli arazi araçları pazarında yeni bir alternatif oluşturuyor.

source_texts.title: The Obstacles of Low Range and High Price: 2026 Jeep Recon EV Tested
source_texts.summary: Quick and trail-rated, the Recon offers a Wrangler-adjacent lifestyle with some EV benefits—and some EV baggage.
source_texts.text:
10/02/26 UPDATE: This review has been updated with instrumented test results.
Feeling beaten down by work and the urban grind? You need a bath. A forest bath. Despite what it sounds like, “forest bathing” is not the act of washing up among the trees. No loofahs or bathtubs are required. Shinrin-yoku is a wellness trend that started in Japan and is finding global interest among nature lovers who need a break from more extreme outdoors activities. It’s not about exercise or competition so much as letting the dappled light and loamy air of serene surroundings wash away the hustle and grime of big-city life.
The 2026 Jeep Recon would be an excellent vehicle for forest bathing, not because it’s incapable of challenging off-roading, but because its electric powertrain and open-air cabin options are so well suited to a gentle exploration. It’s also stonking quick if you’re not into every aspect of the slow life, with a not-so-zen 670 horsepower and 620 pound-feet of torque.
The Recon looks like the Wranglers and Cherokees of yore with a boxy profile, square headlights, and a lit-up, modernized version of the classic seven-slot Jeep grille. It shares a platform with the currently on-pause Jeep Wagoneer S, making it a little longer than the classic Jeep, at 193.3 inches overall against a four-door Wrangler Unlimited’s 188.4 inches. Unlike the more luxury-focused Wagoneer S, the Recon is chunky and rugged, offering off-road-friendly stats like 9.1 inches of ground clearance, a 33.8-degree approach angle, a 33.1-degree departure angle, and a 23.3-degree breakover angle.
The Recon will clear obstacles in a hurry thanks to two 335-hp electric motors (providing all-wheel drive) paired with a 94-kWh battery. The combo is good for a 3.6-second sprint to 60 mph by the manufacturer’s estimate. At our test track, it was even quicker, zipping to 60 mph in 3.5 seconds and clearing the quarter-mile mark in 11.8 seconds at 111 mph. And that quarter-mile time is held back substantially by the amusing fact that the Recon hits its 111-mph top speed more than a second before the 1320-foot mark arrives. Did we mention it’s on 33-inch all-terrain tires? On the road, the Recon accelerates and merges as if it’s not shaped and weighted like a cinder block, and showing up with one at a drag strip with the doors off and a helmet on would be a hilarious flex.
Along with bringing some speed to the family tree, the Recon also deviates from its Wrangler cousins in steering and handling. There’s none of the wander or wobble that famously bonds Wrangler fans and sends haters to Ford dealers. The Recon tucks into turns and accelerates without a wiggle, although rough roads produced a bit of back-end bounce, an occasional reminder that we were in a vehicle sprung for off-road pursuits. On the skidpad, the Recon pulled 0.74 g, which is more sideways stick than we’ve seen from recent Wrangler variants.
The downside of a bricky design on knobby tires is a thirst for electrons. The Recon only promises 222 miles of estimated range in the Moab trim we drove, and things likely won’t improve much with the upcoming Overland model. Jeep says off-road regen makes the Recon more efficient than it seems on paper, which may be true, but that isn’t as good a selling point as a 300-mile range would be. We didn’t use much juice while bopping up and down on mild fire trails and over a few rocky obstacles, but unless you live up against the border of BLM land, it’s likely you’ll have several hundred miles between you and the closest OHV roads. Back in Michigan, the Recon only covered 160 miles on our 75-mph highway range test before we needed to do some recon on a recharge. That might be fine for commuting around town, but given Jeep’s desire to see these things off the beaten path, there’s something about being out of cell range that makes one more concerned about vehicle range, especially when you can’t strap an extra gallon to the roof rails.
Assuming you don’t mind stopping for a leisurely charge on the way—in our 10 to 90 percent charge test, the Recon took a lackluster 43 minutes, averaging 107 kW—this electric Jeep is a nice setup for a day outside. It’s quick and stable on a mountain road, and with the power top folded all the way back, the cabin fills with sunshine, cold air, and pine. Turn onto a dirt road, maybe stop at a cabin or a campsite, and you can wrestle the doors off for the full open-air experience.
All four doors and the rear windows are removable without tools, which is pretty trick, but at about 70 pounds apiece for the doors, it’s more of a team activity than a solo one. There’s also no easy way to store the doors in the Recon, though the windows come with a cute padded bag and can tuck into the cargo space as long as you’re willing to sacrifice some of the 30 cubic feet of cargo space behind the second row. There’s an additional 3 cubes in the frunk, which is best used for the charging cable or a large bag of trail mix.
Once you’ve found somewhere to store your doors and windows, the stripped-down Recon looks like something you’d find abandoned in a bad part of town. Aesthetics of driving a frame aside, the electric hum, birdsong, and a breeze that goes all the way through make a compelling argument for electric outdoorsing.
The Recon is capable, too, with steel skid plates over the battery, a 15:1 final-drive ratio on the rear axle and an electronically-controlled locking rear differential. On our drive in the Moab trim, we didn’t encounter any wheeling challenges worthy of the name, but the Recon showcased impressive articulation in a series of deep dugouts, swam through a slippery mud pool (it has a 24-inch fording depth), and crawled over the slipperier mud-covered rocks at the exit. There’s no lack of torque or flexibility, but the Recon does exhibit two common off-road EV issues: choppy accelerator response and overly aggressive brakes.
Jeep makes attempts at re-creating the smooth confidence of a low-geared combustion rig with off-road-specific drive modes like Rock and Sand, which change the pedal response and stability control intervention. A separate Creep setting is designed to mimic the slow pull of a torquey engine in low gear, but we found it added too much acceleration, like trying to hold back a car with a too-high idle. When combined with a grabby brake pedal, feathering the Recon into position proved difficult. Despite the overactive feel from the brakes, the Recon takes a sizable 201 feet to halt from 70 mph, and 399 feet to bring it down from 100 mph.
It’s not all complaints here. Thoughtfulness in design has been a part of Jeep’s legacy, and the Recon has some wins along with some spots for improvement. The interior design is roomy and easy to navigate, with interesting seat patterns and fun easter-egg design elements.
